passages.title: The Striking Calamity and the shattered world
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat name the Day of Judgement by one of its most alarming names — **al-Qāriʿah**, "The Striking Disaster" — and then answer the question "what is it?" not with a definition but with two pictures: people scattered like moths, and the mountains like carded wool.

What holds the passage together is a single movement from **name** to **sight**. Ayat 1–3 name the event and magnify it. Ayat 4–5 finally show it, and they show it in two matching strokes: what becomes of people, and what becomes of the earth's most solid features.

## Ayah 1: the name that strikes

The surah opens with a single word: **ٱلۡقَارِعَةُ** — rendered here as "The Striking Disaster." It lands like the blow it names.

Ibn Kathir explains that **al-Qāriʿah is one of the names of the Day of Judgement**, and he lists others alongside it: *al-Ḥāqqah*, *aṭ-Ṭāmmah*, *aṣ-Ṣākhkhah*, *al-Ghāshiyah*, and other names besides. This is worth pausing over. That Day is not given one label in the Qur'an but many, and each name grips it from a different side. Here the chosen name is the one that strikes. Naming it this way is itself the first stage of the warning: before you are told anything about the Day, you are told what it *does*.

## Ayat 2–3: two questions that are not looking for an answer

**Ayah 2** asks, *"What is the Striking Disaster?"* — and notice that the name is not replaced by a pronoun. It is spoken again in full. The word comes at you twice.

**Ayah 3** then goes further: *"And what will make you realize what the Striking Disaster is?"* Ibn Kathir's comment on this is a single sentence, and it is the key to the two questions. After naming the Day, he says, **"Allah intensifies concern and fright for it"** by asking this.

So the questions are not gaps waiting to be filled with a fact. On Ibn Kathir's reading their work is to raise alarm — to press the weight of the thing named onto the hearer rather than to inform him. Whatever you are now picturing is smaller than what is coming.

Then, having lifted the event out of reach, the passage gives you something you *can* picture.

## Ayah 4: people like scattered moths

*"˹It is˺ the Day people will be like scattered moths."*

Ibn Kathir treats this ayah as the explanation that the previous ayat were building toward — "Then He explains this by saying…" — and he spells out exactly where the likeness lies: it is a comparison **"in their scattering, their dividing, their coming and their going, all due to being bewildered at what is happening to them."**

Sit with that list. It is not one motion but four, and none of them goes anywhere. Scattering, splitting apart, coming, going. And Ibn Kathir names the cause plainly: **bewilderment**. They move like that because they cannot take in what is happening to them.

Note also *who* is being described. The word is **an-nās** — people at large; Ibn Kathir's rendering has it as "mankind." Not a nation, not a group. Everyone, moving without order and without arriving.

Ibn Kathir connects this to another ayah where the Qur'an uses the same kind of image, *"As if they were locusts spread abroad"* (54:7) — the same sense of countless creatures spilling outward with no order to them.

## Ayah 5: mountains like carded wool

*"And the mountains will be like carded wool."*

The Arabic is **كَٱلۡعِهۡنِ ٱلۡمَنفُوشِ** — *ʿihn* that has been *manfūsh*. (*Carded* wool is wool combed loose, pulled into fluff.) Ibn Kathir reports that a whole line of the early Qur'an teachers — **Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī** — all glossed *ʿihn* as wool. That is a striking amount of agreement, and it tells you the image is meant to be taken as it stands: wool, plainly.

Ibn Kathir's own explanation adds a further sense to the fluffiness — that of coming apart. The mountains **"will become like carded wool that has began to wear out (fade away) and be torn apart."** So it is not simply that they turn soft. They wear away and are pulled to pieces.

Now put ayah 4 and ayah 5 side by side, because the wording invites it: *people **will be** like…* and *the mountains **will be** like…* — two halves of one scene, built the same way.

- Ayah 4 takes away every human anchor: no crowd holds together, no one is in control of where they are going.
- Ayah 5 takes away the last physical anchor. Mountains are the thing a person assumes will still be standing tomorrow. On that Day they have the substance of combed-out wool, worn away and torn apart.

Between them, these two ayat remove the two things a human being leans on for stability — other people, and the ground itself. That is what "the Striking Disaster" means in practice. It is not merely a loud event. It is the undoing of everything that made you feel settled.

## Where the passage is heading

Ibn Kathir marks the turn himself. Once these two scenes have been given, he says, **"Allah informs about the results received by those who performed the deeds, and the honour and disgrace they will experience based upon their deeds."** The surah does not leave you in the scattering. Having shown the world coming apart, it goes on to what will be true of each person in it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up that continuation in a line: this surah mentions the weighing of human deeds — **"He whose scales are heavy will be led to Paradise, and he whose scales are light will be led to Hell."** That is where ayat 1–5 are pointing; the ayat that follow are where it is spelled out.

## Living it

The most practical thing this passage asks of a believer is a shift in what he counts as solid.

Everything that comes apart in ayat 4–5 is something people currently treat as fixed: the crowd you belong to, your bearings among other people, the standing mountains of a world you are making plans inside of. The passage does not ask you to despise these things. It asks you to stop mistaking them for anchors, because you have now been told in advance what becomes of them.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a principle worth carrying away from a surah about weight: **on the Day of Judgement human deeds will not be counted, but weighed.** It puts it plainly — fewer good deeds carried out with a high degree of faith and sincerity and in accordance with the Sunnah will be heavier than many good deeds (prayers, fasting, charity, pilgrimage) performed with a lesser degree of faith and sincerity, or not completely in accordance with the Sunnah.

That is a mercy hidden inside a terrifying passage. A world where deeds are *counted* would belong to whoever had the most time, the most money, the most opportunity. A world where they are *weighed* belongs to whoever brought the most faith and sincerity to what little they had. The mountains will be like carded wool; a small act done truly for Allah will not be.

passages.title: Heavy and light scales, bliss or abyss
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** After the terror of the Day itself has been sounded — the Striking Calamity, mankind like moths scattered about, the mountains like carded wool — these six ayat tell us the outcome. All of humanity is sorted into two columns, decided by one thing: the weight of what a person brings. Ayat 6–7 are the first column, ayat 8–11 the second, and the two are built as mirror halves of a single sentence: *as for the one whose scales are heavy… but as for the one whose scales are light…*

Ibn Kathir marks the turn precisely. After describing the upheaval, Allah then informs about the results received by those who performed the deeds, and the honour and disgrace they will experience based upon their deeds. The cosmic scene narrows to a single human being standing before a balance.

---

## Two columns, one balance

Ayah 6 says *fa-ammā man thaqulat mawāzīnuh* — "Then as for him whose Balance will be heavy." Ibn Kathir gives the plain sense: **his good deeds are more than his bad deeds**. Ayah 8, *wa-ammā man khaffat mawāzīnuh*, is its exact opposite: **his bad deeds are more than his good deeds**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the consequence just as simply: he whose scales are heavy will be led to Paradise, and he whose scales are light will be led to Hell.

So the surah affirms a real weighing of human deeds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this as a settled matter of belief and directs the reader to its own fuller analysis (Ma'ariful Qur'an, Vol. 3, pp. 539–547), which it says both explains the weighing in full and allays the doubts raised against the very concept of deeds being weighed.

## Weighed, not counted

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a principle that changes how a believer thinks about his own record:

> On the Day of Judgment human deeds will not be counted, but weighed.

The difference is enormous. A count rewards volume. A weighing rewards **density**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells it out: fewer good deeds with a high degree of faith and sincerity, and in accordance with the Sunnah, will be heavier than many good deeds — prayers, fasting, charity and pilgrimage — performed with a lesser degree of faith and sincerity, or not completely in accordance with the Sunnah.

The named ingredients of weight, then, are three: the degree of faith, sincerity, and conformity to the Sunnah (the Prophet's ﷺ way of doing a thing). The same outward act can come to the scale heavy or light depending on them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further layer here, and is careful to present it as an inference drawn from reconciling the various narrations and Qur'anic verses, not as a certainty. On that reading, the weighing on the Plain of Resurrection will take place **twice**:

- **The first weighing** separates the believers from the non-believers. Anyone whose Book of Deeds is put on the scale and contains belief (*īmān*) will be heavy; the scale of anyone whose Ledger of Deeds does not contain *īmān* will be light.
- **The second weighing** distinguishes between the good and evil deeds of the believers.

The reference in this surah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is *probably* to the first weighing — in which the scale of every believer will be heavy regardless of his other deeds, while the scale of an unbeliever will be light even though he might have performed some good acts. Note the word *probably*: it is offered as a considered reading, and it stands alongside Ibn Kathir's more direct reading of ayah 6 as good deeds outweighing bad.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites **Mazharī** on a related point: the Qur'an, when speaking of reward and punishment, generally contrasts the unbelievers with the *righteous* believers, because the latter are the perfect believers. As for the believers who have performed righteous as well as unrighteous deeds, the Qur'an is generally silent on the issue. It is immediately after saying this that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the principle above — that deeds are weighed and not counted. Where the Qur'an does not spell out a case, the believer is handed a measure to work with.

## Bliss and abyss

**The heavy scale.** *Fa-huwa fī ʿīshatin rāḍiyah* — "He will live a pleasant life." Ibn Kathir's explanation is a single phrase, and it is the only one needed: **in Paradise**.

**The light scale.** *Fa-ummuhu hāwiyah* — "His mother will be Hāwiyah." This is the strangest expression in the surah, and Ibn Kathir reports two ways it has been understood. He does not force a choice between them.

*First view — the head-first fall.* It has been said that this means he will be falling and tumbling headfirst into the fire of Hell, the expression "his mother" being used to refer to his brain, as it is the mother of his head. A statement similar to this has been reported from **Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Abū Ṣāliḥ and Qatādah**. Qatādah said, "He will fall into the Hellfire on his head." Abū Ṣāliḥ made a similar statement: "They will fall into the Fire on their heads." On this reading the image is a body pitched over an edge — and *Hāwiyah* carries the sense of a plunging fall, the "abyss" of the translation.

*Second view — Hāwiyah as the abode.* It has also been said that the mother he will return to and end up with in the Hereafter is Hāwiyah, which is one of the names of the Hellfire. **Ibn Jarīr** explained the metaphor exactly: "Al-Hāwiyah is only called his mother because he will have no other abode except for it." **Ibn Zayd** said, "Al-Hāwiyah is the Fire, and it will be his mother and his abode to which he will return, and where he will be settled" — and he recited, *"Their abode will be the Fire"* (3:151). **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** narrated from Qatādah that it is the Fire, and it is their abode.

Sit with what that second reading does. A mother is where a person comes from, where he is taken in, the place he returns to when everything else fails. The ayah takes that word — the warmest word a human being knows — and hands it to the Fire. For the one whose scale was light, there is no home left in existence but that one. The tenderness of the metaphor is precisely what makes it devastating.

## The question, and the answer

*Wa mā adrāka mā hiyah* — "And what will make you realize what that is?" This is the second time the surah uses this construction; ayah 3 used it of Al-Qāriʿah itself, and Ibn Kathir notes the effect there: by asking it, Allah intensifies concern and fright for it. Here Ibn Kathir presents the question as Allah's own way of explaining the meaning of Al-Hāwiyah — so the answer arrives in the next breath.

*Nārun ḥāmiyah* — "A fire Hāmiyah!" Ibn Kathir explains: **extreme heat**. It is a heat that is accompanied by a strong flame and fire. He then brings a series of narrations that translate that word into something the human body can feel.

- It is narrated from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The fire of the Children of Adam that you all kindle is one part of the seventy parts of the fire of Hell." They (the Companions) said, "O Messenger of Allah! Isn't it sufficient?" He replied, "It is more than it by sixty-nine times." **This has been recorded by Al-Bukhārī and Muslim.** In some of the wordings he added, "each of them is like the heat of it."

  Take that in. Every burn you have ever flinched from is the mildest sample. The surah's *ḥāmiyah* begins where your experience ends.

- It has been narrated in a Hadith that **Imam Aḥmad** recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Verily, the person who will receive the lightest torment of the people of the Hellfire will be a man who will have two sandals that will cause his brain to boil." The *lightest*.

- It has been **confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the Hellfire complained to its Lord and said, "O Lord! Some parts of me devour other parts of me." So Allah permitted it to take two breaths, one in the winter and one in the summer; thus the most severe cold you experience in winter is from its cold, and the most severe heat you experience in summer is from its heat.

- And **in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs** it is recorded that he ﷺ said, "When the heat becomes intense pray the prayer when it cools down, for indeed the intense heat is from the breath of Hell."

That last one is remarkable for how ordinary it is. A ruling about when to pray — the sort of practical instruction a Muslim follows without thinking — is anchored to the reality named in ayah 11. The Fire is not filed away in a distant chapter of the future; the Sunnah lets a hot afternoon remind you of it.

---

## Living it

Read as a whole, ayat 6–11 leave a believer with three things to carry.

**Weigh, don't count.** Since the scale measures weight and not number, the question to ask of your worship is not *how much* but *how heavy*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names what adds the weight: the degree of faith, sincerity, and conformity to the Sunnah. Prayer, fasting, charity, pilgrimage — the very acts it lists — can come to the scale light if those are thin, or heavy if they are full. This is the most practical instruction in the surah, and it is available to everyone: you cannot always add hours, but you can always add sincerity.

**Guard what makes the scale heavy at all.** On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of the first weighing, it is *īmān* in the ledger that gives it weight; a record without it stays light however much good it contains. Faith is not one item among the deeds; it is what gives the deeds their density.

**Let the fear be real.** Ibn Kathir spends his commentary on ayah 11 making sure you do not read *ḥāmiyah* as a word on a page. But note where the passage begins — with the heavy scale and the pleasant life. The one facing the abyss of ayah 9 has already been shown, in ayat 6 and 7, what leads elsewhere: a scale made heavy quietly, deed by sincere deed, before the Striking ever came.
